vignette:
She is sixty-nine now, a North American woman who has spent most of her life working outdoors, reading weather in the sky and soil with the ease other people read clocks. She is married, and for decades she has worked alongside her husband in agriculture, rising before daylight, pulling on work clothes in the dark, and heading out to fields and barns with the steady discipline of someone who has always believed that hard work keeps life in order. When she speaks about the assault, she does not begin with the word itself. She begins with the season, the smell of fertilizer, the feeling of grit on the back of her neck, the fact that she had stayed late to finish a task that normally would have waited until morning.

At the time, she is in her fifties and used to being alone on the property. She knows the routines of deliveries, repairs, neighboring workers coming and going. The man is someone close enough to the farm not to seem alarming at first. She remembers the ordinary shape of the evening more vividly than she remembers his face. She is bent over her work, tired, thinking about getting inside before dark, when the ordinary day turns all at once. Later, what torments her is how quickly her body understands danger before her mind can catch up. She remembers freezing, the disbelief giving way to terror, and then the strange detached clarity of noticing small things—the pressure of the ground, the smell of hay, a far-off engine—while feeling herself disappear inside. During the assault, she thinks, with shame that still lives in her, that if she can just survive the next minute, then the next, she might get home.

Afterward, she does get home, but she does not feel as if she has returned. She scrubs herself until her skin burns. She cannot bear her husband touching her, even gently, and when he asks what is wrong, she says she is tired, that she pulled a muscle, that she does not want to talk. The words lodge in her throat. She has spent her life being capable, and now she feels contaminated, furious, and deeply embarrassed by what was done to her. She tells herself she should have fought harder, should have known, should not have been there alone. The self-blame settles in quickly and stays.

In the months that follow, she keeps working because that is what she knows to do. She feeds animals, checks irrigation, sorts produce, signs invoices, but her body is never simply doing those tasks anymore. She startles at footsteps behind her. If a truck she does not recognize turns into the drive, her heart begins pounding so hard she feels lightheaded. She starts scanning every doorway and field edge without meaning to. At night she lies awake listening for sounds outside, replaying the assault in sudden, unwanted flashes that feel less like memories than like being dragged backward into it. Some nights she wakes from dreams gasping, convinced for a few seconds that he is in the room. Her husband reaches for her and she jerks away before she knows who he is.

She becomes someone she barely recognizes. She avoids the part of the property where it happened, then rearranges chores so she never has to be there at all. When avoidance becomes impossible, she steels herself for hours beforehand and is shaky for the rest of the day. She stops attending community gatherings she once enjoyed because she cannot tolerate men standing too close or people asking casual questions about how she is doing. The world narrows. She tells herself she prefers to be alone, but in quieter moments she knows she is living as if danger is waiting just out of sight.

Her marriage changes under the strain. Her husband knows something terrible has happened long before she finally tells him, but the secrecy creates its own distance. When she does speak, it comes out in fragments, with long silences in between. She watches his face as she talks, afraid he will see her differently. Even after he responds with care, she remains guarded. Intimacy becomes tangled with panic. There are times she wants comfort and cannot tolerate being held. She hates what that does to both of them, and the guilt deepens her isolation.

Now, years later, the assault still organizes her days more than she wants to admit. She is older, her body slower from the ordinary wear of farm work and age, but the alarm in her nervous system feels untouched by time. She is exhausted by how much effort it takes to appear normal. She keeps busy because stillness invites memories. She avoids news stories about violence, avoids certain roads, avoids being alone with men she does not know well. Loud voices, the smell of diesel mixed with summer heat, the scrape of boots behind her can make her feel instantly cornered. On those days she becomes irritable and withdrawn, then ashamed of that too.

What she grieves most is not only the assault itself but the theft of her sense of safety in a life that had once felt sturdy and familiar. The farm remains the center of her world, yet even there she is never fully at ease. She speaks about wanting just one ordinary day in which she can walk across her own land without bracing herself, without listening for danger, without being carried back to that evening against her will.
